notes.bp: Speech in noise may depend on acoustic information above the frequency range normally used by speech systems.
notes.wh: High-frequency cues can be masked, and an ASR result does not automatically explain why a human listener benefits from them.
notes.naive: Discard everything above 6–8 kHz because it is assumed irrelevant to phonemes.
notes.ap: Use a phoneme recognizer as a controlled probe of which frequency bands help under masking and spatial separation.
notes.mech: A neural network decodes phonemes from cochleagrams of broadband, 8-kHz-low-pass, and 6-kHz-low-pass speech under quiet and masked conditions.
notes.math: Recognition accuracy and phoneme-omission probabilities are compared across target-to-masker ratios, filtering conditions, and consonant/vowel classes.
notes.dots: The model is a probe for an acoustic cue, not proof that it hears like a person.
notes.ww: Broadband speech improves phoneme accuracy in masked conditions, especially at lower TMR, while adding no quiet-condition benefit; removing extended high frequencies increases consonant omissions.
notes.limits: VCTK speech, selected maskers, cochleagram assumptions, and a model-based probe bound the conclusion; audiological benefit and general ASR deployment are not established.

notes.bp: Echo cancellation must work when the room's echo path differs from anything seen during training.
notes.wh: The echo path is hidden, changes with geometry, and can be noisy when measured; double talk makes suppression without near-end damage harder.
notes.naive: Train on synthetic mixtures and assume the learned filter generalizes to every room.
notes.ap: Give the model a room impulse response as a prompt so it can condition cancellation on acoustic structure at test time.
notes.mech: ICCRN receives several RIR-prompt fusion variants; tests cover matched and mismatched synthetic RIRs plus recorded real RIRs in double-talk and far-end single-talk conditions.
notes.math: ERLE measures echo suppression, PESQ near-end quality, SDR near-end fidelity, and MACs/parameters expose the prompt cost.
notes.dots: The room response becomes an explicit conditioning variable instead of an unobserved nuisance.
notes.ww: Fusion method (d) is strongest on mismatched and real-RIR ICCRN tests; the reported real-RIR double-talk values are PESQ 2.19 and ERLE 4.79.
notes.limits: The selected model, fusion choices, RIRs, and author-reported tables bound the claim; independent reproduction and broad room coverage remain absent.

notes.bp: Long transcripts are easier to use when topics are organized into nested sections rather than one flat stream.
notes.wh: Spoken transcripts lack visible chapters, boundaries are ambiguous, and coarse and fine topic changes must be represented across languages and recordings.
notes.naive: Predict one boundary label at each position and evaluate only whether a nearby cut is correct.
notes.ap: Generate a hierarchical table of contents and use a metric that respects its levels; add pause duration only when training can use it.
notes.mech: TOC-NEMO uses LoRA fine-tuning and optional pause cues on AMI, VideoAula, and LectureDE; zero-shot prompting and supervised baselines provide comparisons.
notes.math: Linear F1/B and hierarchical B distinguish flat boundary quality from agreement across levels; bootstrap and leave-one-speaker-out averages are reported.
notes.dots: A boundary's meaning depends on the level of organization it creates, not only its time location.
notes.ww: Fine-tuned TOC-NEMO plus pause cues reports the strongest linear scores, including AMI F1 30.34/B 24.81 and VideoAula F1 67.34/B 55.18.
notes.limits: Datasets, prompts, annotations, and metric behavior constrain the result; transcript segmentation is not proof of human topic understanding.

notes.bp: A useful device speech generator must be intelligible, natural, fast enough for streaming, and usable across speakers.
notes.wh: Codec TTS often predicts several discrete code levels sequentially, making large models slow even when waveform quality is good.
notes.naive: Use a large autoregressive decoder and accept long latency, or predict code levels independently and lose their dependencies.
notes.ap: Use a Mamba acoustic model with depthwise residual-codec decoding: masked refinement preserves dependencies, while implicit neural representation predicts levels in parallel.
notes.mech: SMAM is tested with MLM, INR, and no-MLM decoding in a zero-shot speaker-conditioned setup; CER, similarity, quality, real-time factor, latency, and listening scores separate tradeoffs.
notes.math: MLM reports 26M parameters, CER 2.73, RTF 0.701, latency 0.065 s, MOS 4.02, and SMOS 3.36; INR uses 25M parameters and RTF 0.568 with latency 0.061 s.
notes.dots: This is structured prediction under a time budget: preserving codec dependencies improves quality while parallel prediction improves speed.
notes.ww: The proposed models are smaller and faster than listed non-streaming baselines while remaining competitive; removing MLM degrades quality measures.
notes.limits: Codec, datasets, hardware, and zero-shot speaker conditions bound the conclusion; other languages and devices are not established.

notes.bp: Reading fluency assessment should capture accuracy, smoothness, phrasing, and pacing without manually scoring every child.
notes.wh: ASR and timing errors can corrupt the educational measure, and agreement with transcript proxies is not the same as instructional validity.
notes.naive: Use words-correct-per-minute alone or treat an accurate transcript as sufficient evidence that every fluency measure is valid.
notes.ap: Extract fifteen measures from ASR transcripts and timings, then compare them with the same measures from human transcripts.
notes.mech: The study evaluates 244 recordings from 131 Dutch children aged 6–13, compares four ASR systems, and correlates automatic and human-derived fluency measures.
notes.math: WER, timing F1, and Pearson correlations quantify separate links from audio to educational measure; 12 of 15 measures show strong correlations.
notes.dots: An automatic metric is useful only if its errors preserve the human construct being measured.
notes.ww: The best reported system has WER 12.3% and timing F1 0.82; twelve measures meet r ≥ 0.7.
notes.limits: Dutch child reading, fixed texts, age distribution, ASR choice, and transcript comparison limit generalization; intervention or diagnosis validity is not established.

notes.bp: Spoken-language understanding must fit on a device with limited memory and power without losing needed intent and slot decisions.
notes.wh: Pruning can remove rare but important vocabulary or acoustic layers, while average scores can hide task-specific loss.
notes.naive: Shrink a model uniformly or remove the smallest weights without asking which tokens and layers support the task.
notes.ap: Prune task-irrelevant vocabulary first, prune layers structurally, then refine with distillation and contrastive losses.
notes.mech: PruneSLU starts from Whisper-tiny, selects a base vocabulary, chooses layers by loss, and trains with language-model, distillation, and contrastive components on STOP and SLURP.
notes.math: Exact match, EM-Tree, intent accuracy, slot F1, parameter counts, and pruning/loss ablations expose the tradeoff.
notes.dots: Deployment is constrained optimization: retained representation must preserve task structure, not merely parameter magnitude.
notes.ww: The 15M model retains 98% of original STOP performance, reaches STOP EM 72.31 and SLURP slot F1 71.42, and improves on listed compression baselines.
notes.limits: STOP/SLURP domains, Whisper initialization, five seeds, and author-reported comparisons bound the result; energy and open-world commands are not tested.

notes.bp: A quality predictor should approximate what listeners hear without requiring a listening test for every utterance.
notes.wh: Ratings are noisy, quality depends on local defects and whole-utterance context, and large encoders make prediction impractical.
notes.naive: Train a large model on MOS labels and treat every listener score as equally reliable.
notes.ap: Use attention for local and global context in a small model, then sequentially teach it from refined targets to reduce noisy-rating effects.
notes.mech: AttentiveMOS uses Swin and transformer attention with 86K parameters and is evaluated across in-domain, out-of-domain, and cross-domain MOS datasets.
notes.math: MSE measures rating error while Pearson and Spearman measure agreement; SOMOS-clean reports MSE 0.257, PCC 0.449, and SRCC 0.442.
notes.dots: A metric predictor is itself a deployment model whose compactness and domain shift must be measured alongside correlation.
notes.ww: It beats listed lightweight baselines in the reported SOMOS-clean comparison, but PCC falls to 0.359 on out-of-domain LIVETALK.
notes.limits: MOS labels, listener composition, dataset domains, and the sharp shift drop limit claims of general quality assessment.

notes.bp: A codec can sound pleasant yet make words harder to understand, so intelligibility needs its own evaluation target.
notes.wh: Quality scores and WER can miss phoneme-specific distortions and listener-dependent effects, especially for generative codecs.
notes.naive: Use MOS or WER as a universal proxy for whether listeners identify speech sounds.
notes.ap: Provide a standardized rhyme-test toolkit and compare its subjective results with objective intelligibility measures.
notes.mech: SITool runs Diagnostic and Modified Rhyme Tests in laboratory or crowdsourcing settings; thirteen codecs are evaluated with phoneme, gender, and wordlist analyses.
notes.math: Subjective scores are compared with STOI, ESTOI, and WER; only STOI and ESTOI significantly correlate in the reported analysis.
notes.dots: The target determines the metric: intelligibility is not interchangeable with naturalness or transcription accuracy.
notes.ww: Some neural codecs outperform traditional codecs in subjective intelligibility, but objective agreement varies and scores show gender- and wordlist-specific differences.
notes.limits: The codec set, English tests, listener screening, and objective metrics bound the conclusion; the toolkit does not remove human evaluation.
